title: Detecting Filesystem Capability Laundering in MCP Servers at Scale
content:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security
  [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026]
Title:My Credentials, Please: Detecting Filesystem Capability Laundering in MCP Servers at Scale
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how AI agents invoke external tools. MCP servers expose tools through a declared contract consisting of a name, description, and argument schema. In typical local deployments, client-side approval of a tool call grants the underlying server process broad host filesystem permissions rather than restricting it to the declared operation. We study the resulting vulnerability class, filesystem capability laundering, where attacker-steered arguments cause a tool to access sensitive host files outside its declared contract and deployment scope. We analyze this capability gap across three layers: server-category screening (L1), per-tool contract analysis (L2), and bypassable path-validation checks (L3). We design MCP-FSD to catalog MCP servers, infer least-privilege boundaries per tool, plant credential fixtures outside those boundaries, and evaluate exploitability and sandbox containment via paired dynamic execution. Across 21,097 MCP servers from nine registries, 787 of 4,806 triaged servers (16.4%) exhibit filesystem capabilities despite non-filesystem functional classifications. Dynamic three-case validation confirms 150 vulnerable instances under tested sandbox policies. Coordinated disclosure yielded 13 security advisories, including two CVEs in Anthropic's Git MCP Server.

report.summary: A large-scale study finds 16.4% of triaged MCP servers can be steered into reading host files outside their declared scope, exposing credentials.
report.background: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become the de facto standard for connecting AI agents to external tools, and thousands of community servers now populate public registries. Each server advertises a contract — a tool name, description, and argument schema — that clients display to users for approval. The problem is architectural: approval is granted to the server process, not scoped to the declared operation, so a process that legitimately needs one file can typically reach anything the host user can. Combined with prompt injection and attacker-controlled tool arguments, this turns benign utilities into confused-deputy channels. Prior MCP security work focused on tool poisoning, rug pulls, and prompt injection through descriptions; this paper isolates a distinct, measurable vulnerability class — filesystem capability laundering — and builds tooling to find it across the ecosystem at registry scale.
key_points: The root cause is a permission-model mismatch. When a user approves an MCP tool call, the client typically grants the whole server process the host filesystem rights of the user account, not the narrow operation described in the tool's contract. Any tool with an argument that becomes a path can therefore be redirected at sensitive files such as SSH keys, cloud credentials, or .env secrets.

The scale is substantial. The authors cataloged 21,097 MCP servers across nine registries and triaged 4,806 of them; 787 (16.4%) demonstrated filesystem access capabilities despite being classified as non-filesystem tools. That means servers marketed as search, database, or utility helpers can still touch local disks.

MCP-FSD is the detection framework. It analyzes capability gaps at three layers — server-category screening, per-tool contract analysis, and bypassable path-validation checks — then infers least-privilege boundaries, plants credential fixtures outside them, and runs paired dynamic executions to confirm exploitability and measure sandbox containment.

Dynamic validation confirmed real exposure. Three-case dynamic testing identified 150 confirmed vulnerable instances under the sandbox policies tested, showing that static schema anomalies translate into working file-read primitives rather than theoretical risk.

Disclosure produced concrete fixes. Coordinated disclosure yielded 13 security advisories, including two CVEs in Anthropic's Git MCP Server — notable because it is a first-party, widely used reference implementation rather than an obscure community package.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the paper reframes MCP trust as a capability problem rather than a documentation problem: approval dialogs that grant process-wide access are structurally unsafe, and registries will likely need capability attestation or signed manifests. Vendors should expect pressure to adopt operation-scoped permissions and sandbox-by-default execution. For developers, argument validation is now security-critical — canonicalize paths, allowlist directories, and never let model-supplied strings reach the filesystem unchecked; assuming a sandbox is sufficient is explicitly challenged by the bypass findings. For regular users, installing an MCP server is closer to running an unvetted local binary than installing a browser extension; running servers in containers with only the directories they need mounted is the practical mitigation.
report.tools: Watch the paper's MCP-FSD artifact for registry-scale scanning and least-privilege inference. For hands-on testing, use the official MCP Inspector to review tool schemas and arguments, plus Semgrep or CodeQL rules for path-construction sinks in server code. For containment, run servers in Docker/devcontainers with narrow volume mounts, or use gVisor, bubblewrap, or firejail with seccomp profiles. Keeping an audit trail of approved tool calls and their arguments also helps catch laundering attempts early.
